title: Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification
summary: The paper proposes fastText, a linear text classifier that embeds words plus hashed word n-grams, averages them into a small hidden vector (h=10), and feeds a linear softmax layer trained by SGD with a linearly decaying learning rate. It is evaluated with one fixed hyperparameter set on the 8 sentiment benchmarks of Zhang et al. (2015) and on the 312K-class YFCC100M tag-prediction task, where it matches or approaches char-CNN/char-CRNN/VDCNN accuracy while being orders of magnitude faster on a CPU. The headline result targeted here is 92.5% test accuracy on AG News with h=10 and bigrams (vs. 91.5% with unigrams alone), at ~1 s per training epoch.

match_target.why: The user hint names exactly this cell (Table 1, AG News, fastText h=10 with bigrams, 92.5%). It is the paper's central sentiment result at its cheapest: a 4-class dataset with a 7,600-example test set that trains in seconds on a CPU, and it demonstrates the bigram gain over the 91.5% unigram baseline (C2).

tolerance.why: Rule 2: the metric is accuracy-like, printed by the paper as a percentage, on a test set of 7,600 AG News examples (>=2,000; size per the Zhang et al. 2015 protocol the paper adopts), and no std/CI over repeated runs is reported for this value, so the band is 1.0 absolute percentage point.

requirements.stmt: Implement the fastText architecture: embedding look-up matrix A over words and n-gram features, averaged into a hidden vector of dimension 10, followed by a linear output layer B.
requirements.quote: The features are embedded and averaged to form the hidden variable.

requirements.stmt: Train by minimizing negative log-likelihood (softmax cross-entropy) over the predefined classes.
requirements.quote: We use the softmax function f to compute the probability distribution over the predefined classes.

requirements.stmt: The text representation is the (normalized) bag of features: feature embeddings are averaged, then fed to the linear classifier.
requirements.quote: then averaged into a text representation, which is in turn fed to a linear classifier

requirements.stmt: Optimize with stochastic gradient descent and a linearly decaying learning rate; the paper uses asynchronous multi-thread CPU training.
requirements.quote: using stochastic gradient descent and a linearly decaying learning rate

requirements.stmt: Use exactly 10 hidden units for the Table 1 results (both unigram and bigram rows).
requirements.quote: It has 10 hidden units and we evaluate it with and without bigrams.
We use 10 hidden units and run fastText for 5 epochs

requirements.stmt: Select the initial learning rate from the fixed grid {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5} using a validation set (not the test set).
Add word bigram features via the hashing trick with 10M bins for the bigrams-only setting (100M bins otherwise), using the hashing function of Mikolov et al. (2011).
requirements.quote: and 10M bins if we only used bigrams, and 100M otherwise

requirements.stmt: Use the 8 datasets and train/test evaluation protocol of Zhang et al. (2015) and report test accuracy in %.
requirements.quote: We employ the same 8 datasets and evaluation protocol of Zhang et al. (2015).

requirements.stmt: Do not use pre-trained word embeddings; all representations are learned from scratch on the classification task.
requirements.quote: Unlike Tang et al. (2015), fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings

requirements.stmt: Hierarchical softmax is only required for large output spaces (e.g., YFCC100M); for AG News (4 classes) a plain softmax is consistent with the paper.
requirements.quote: When the number of classes is large, computing the linear classifier is computationally expensive.

requirements.stmt: Use the same hyperparameters across all 8 sentiment datasets (no per-dataset tuning except the lr grid on validation).
requirements.quote: FastText has been run with the same parameters for all the datasets.

data.how_to_get: Original release linked from Zhang & LeCun (2015) arXiv:1502.01710 (Google Drive folder); fast.ai mirror: https://s3.amazonaws.com/fast-ai-nlp/ag_news_csv.tgz

stated_compute: Both char-CNN and VDCNN are trained on a NVIDIA Tesla K40 GPU, while our models are trained on a CPU using 20 threads. Table 2 reports 1 s per epoch for fastText h=10 bigram on AG (up to 10 s/epoch on Amazon P.); the abstract adds training happens on a 'standard multicore CPU'.
